orthodox

OR-thuh-doks — ends like 'docks'; orthodox thinkers stay at the docks instead of sailing off into strange new ideas. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Orthodox is following traditional, widely accepted beliefs or practices.

Her orthodox approach to baking meant no shortcuts and no substitutions from her grandmother's recipes.

Example

A doctor sees a patient with a common infection. She prescribes the orthodox treatment — exactly what the medical textbooks recommend, the standard medicine at the standard dose. Any physician in the country would have done the same.

She is sticking to the accepted, standard way of doing things. Unlike 'old-fashioned,' which implies something outdated, an orthodox method is still the recognized norm today.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

traditional: Traditional means following long-established customs — ways of doing things handed down over generations. Orthodox means matching what a field's authorities currently accept as the standard. A therapy approved last year can already be orthodox, while a folk remedy can stay traditional forever without ever becoming orthodox.

conventional: Conventional means conforming to accepted standards — the usual, expected way most people do something. Orthodox is stronger and more official: the approach a field's experts and texts recognize as correct doctrine. A conventional choice is simply customary; an orthodox one carries the backing of established authority.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

unconventional: not conforming to accepted ways

radical: favoring extreme or complete change

Where it sits · how unquestionable the practice has become

common → orthodox → dogmatic

common vs. orthodox: Common is weaker than orthodox — a common practice is merely widespread, while an orthodox one carries the weight of official, established acceptance.

dogmatic vs. orthodox: Dogmatic is stronger than orthodox: an orthodox thinker follows accepted beliefs, but a dogmatic one rigidly insists those beliefs are beyond all question.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ortho-: straight, correct (Greek)

root — dox-: opinion, belief (Greek)

Put it together: Greek ortho- (correct) plus doxa (opinion) literally means 'correct opinion.' Orthodox describes beliefs and practices a community considers the right, standard ones.

Use the root in a new word: paradox: Zeno's most famous paradox still gets argued about in philosophy classes.
